title: The indifference they mean is not equilibrium but the real power of acting and not acting
source_text: XLIII. Porro Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae per indifferentiam illam quae libertatis essentiam, vel constituit, vel saltem necessario sequitur, significare nolunt eum voluntatis statum in quo inter duo opposita nutat, neque ad unum magis inclinat quam ad alterum; sed in aequilibrio quodammodo suspensa, paulo momento huc & illuc impellitur. Agnoscunt enim libertatem in eo reperiri qui ad agendum eo sensu minime est indifferens; sed cujus voluntas alte impressis habitibus ad certas actiones vehementer inclinata est, quique firmum propositum habet sic & non aliter agendi, a quo non nisi aegre admodum dimoveri potest. Sed indifferentia illa in qua, ex eorum mente, sita est arbitrii libertas, non aliud est quam vera potestas agendi & non agendi, quae manet etiam in eo qui fixo & constanti mentis, & voluntatis proposito ad agendum determinatus est.
pass_a_gloss: Further, the Doctors of the Roman Church by that indifference which either constitutes the essence of liberty, or at least necessarily follows it, do not wish to signify that state of the will in which it wavers between two opposites, and inclines no more to one than to the other; but suspended in a certain way in equilibrium, is driven hither and thither by a slight weight. For they acknowledge liberty to be found in him who in that sense is not at all indifferent to acting; but whose will is vehemently inclined to certain actions by deeply impressed habits, and who has a firm purpose of acting so and not otherwise, from which he cannot be moved except very hardly. But that indifference in which, in their mind, liberty of choice is placed, is nothing else than a true power of acting and not acting, which remains even in him who is determined to acting by a fixed and constant purpose of mind and will.
pass_b_english: When the teachers of the Roman Church speak of the indifference that either makes up the essence of freedom or at least necessarily goes with it, they do not mean a state in which the will wavers between two opposites, leaning no more to one than to the other, hanging as if in balance and pushed this way and that by the slightest weight.

They grant that freedom is present in someone who is not at all indifferent in that sense. His will may be strongly inclined to certain actions by deeply rooted habits, and he may have a settled purpose of acting this way and no other, from which he can be moved only with great difficulty.

The indifference in which, in their view, freedom of choice lies is nothing else than a real power of acting and not acting. It remains even in someone whose mind and will are fixed on acting by a firm and steady purpose.

lemmas.gloss: a true power of acting and not acting

choices.why: Kept as in the preceding locus on free choice in general, so the Roman and Reformed accounts are compared in one vocabulary.
